speechtext:
I would ask the Prime Minister a question of which I have given him notice. Would he be good enough to consider, in connection with social security and the Beveridge report, following the practice of the mother of parliaments, where a committee was appointed but where they had a two-days' debate in the house before the committee met? On the govern-

Social Security
ment benches here there are splendid men who have come up from the municipalities and who are well qualified to discuss this question. I think it would be well to do what was done in Great Britain and give members of the house an opportunity to express their opinions in a non-political debate which might form a chart for the course to be taken by the committee.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SUGGESTED OPPORTUNITY FOR DISCUSSION PRIOR TO MEETING OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon.
friend sent me a communication indicating that he intended raising this question. I must say that the more I have considered it the more I feel that it would not be advisable to act upon the suggestion of my hon. friend to have a debate upon the Beveridge report in this house before the matter of social security is referred to a special committee. My hon. friend has just said that the mother of parliaments has followed a certain course. That course, as I take it, was to discuss at Westminster a report which related to the conditions in the United Kingdom. That would be quite proper. But the Beveridge report does not relate, except so far as general principles are involved, to conditions as they exist in this country. In Great Britain most of the matters which are referred to in the Beveridge report come before only one government. In Canada social security is a matter controlled in part by the federal government, in part by the provincial governments. I think it would be wholly advisable that a committee of this house should have the opportunity of considering that aspect of the broad question of social security before we begin a debate on any one particular report.
May I draw my hon. friend's attention to the fact that, in the notice I have given for the appointment of a committee on social security, I expressly request the house to permit the committee to examine and study social insurance policies of other countries. Social insurance policies of other countries will include the Beveridge report. I would think it would be preferable that a discussion of the Beveridge report, so far as it is desirable to have it in this house, would come after members of the committee had had an opportunity of familiarizing themselves with the report.
But there is an even stronger objection to proceeding along the lines which my hon. friend has indicated. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) is anxious to proceed as soon as may be possible with the war appropriation for the coming year. The minister is also anxious to place before the
country, as soon as he can, the budget, so that the people of Canada may have an appreciation of what is involved in the recommendations which the minister will have later to make to the house with respect to the ways and means of raising the revenues required. To proceed with a debate on the Beveridge report before these all-important war measures-because the budget will be that in considerable part as well-are considered by the house would, I think, place an entirely wrong emphasis on the importance of the matters which should be considered at this time, or first of all in this parliament.
I want to take advantage of this moment to say to my hon. friend and to the house-
I said it before, and I wish to repeat iU- that there is a great danger of hon. members of the house and of people throughout the country getting the impression that this war is going to be won in the course of this year, and that what we have most to be concerned about at the present time is what is going to happen after the war, rather than before the war itself is won.
I do not believe it is possible to emphasize too strongly with respect to the progress of the war, the serious situation which exists at this moment, and which lies ahead. As yet there has been no invasion of Europe by armed forces of the allied powers, and up to now Germany continues to control the countries which she has already conquered. She is being driven back at the present time by Russia; but apart from that, the whole problem of the war, as to when and how the axis powers are to be defeated, still remains something which is completely unsolved. It is going to take all the efforts that all the allied powers can make to win the war in the course of a very considerable time. I believe that the more we impress that upon the people of this country, the better it will be for the good of all. If this house begins to take up at the beginning of a session discussions of a post-war matter, before we have even had an opportunity to discuss our war measures, I am sure we would be setting a wholly false example and would be conveying a wholly wrong impression to the country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, February 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. W. E. Harris (Grey-Bruce) for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session and the amendment thereto of Mr. Graydon, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In taking part in this debate at this late stage, my intention is not to take up the time of the house except to make comments which I feel it is my duty to make upon two or three points only.
I shall attempt to be as brief as possible in dealing with three summary outlines, namely, the matter of controls, man-power as affecting agriculture and lumbering, and the social legislation proposed, in comparison to what some of the other countries have already done along this line.
There is no doubt that the various controls which we have set up have been severely criticized by the press and the people of this country, the intensity of this criticism being at times directly proportionate to the curbing of our activities in a given field, industrial, commercial, or again in our habits of life.
We have been so long accustomed to doing things in a democratic way that we resent being told what to do and what not to do. However, no government, not even one which perchance my hon. friend the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Graydon) might lead, could successfully carry out the activities looking to the winning of this war, unless these various controls were resorted to. There is no country at war to-day that has not these controls in its legislation, so that, after all, we Canadians are just doing what every other country is doing to win the war. The men placed at the head of these control boards are for the most part leaders in their respective fields, and I believe that if all of us would be prone to cooperate with them rather than to criticize them, and if we had in view not the one field of a given control as a perspective, but rather, the wider perspective of the whole war picture, perhaps

we would then be contributing a certain unconscious war effort which we at present are not doing.
Perhaps one of the reasons why Canadians have not taken well to some phases of this control is that they have not been sufficiently informed of the reasons why controls of this and that have been established, and perhaps the publicity divisions of our various departments have not explained as fully as they should have done the whys and wherefores for this or that commodity being controlled. Again, some of the newspapers of the country have made a point of criticizing, perhaps too harshly, some of these rationings. I know that there is an enormous difference in the way that these controls are accepted by Canadians and Americans. Living near the border states of New Hampshire, Maine and Vermont, I have occasion to go to border towns quite often throughout the year, and a thought that strikes me on each of my trips thereto is that the Americans, once the government establishes a control or rationing, hardly offer any further criticism. There is hardly any more criticism of that control or rationing by the residents.
To mention one instance of the criticism of rationing, a criticism which we have heard in this house since the beginning, take butter. It might be interesting to know that the present fat ration per capita in Canada is, roughly speaking, 41 pounds per year, consisting of a butter ration of 26 pounds and 15 pounds of other fats. The United States has at present a fat ration of 41 pounds also, but it consists of 17 pounds only of butter, and 24 pounds of other fats. Great Britain has a ration in fats of 26 pounds only, consisting of 6i pounds of butter per year and 13 pounds of vegetable fats, with 6^ pounds of cooking fats. So that after all, although there is a rationing of butter here, our 26 pounds per year per capita is much more than the 17 pounds per year which the American receives, and greater by four times than the 6| pounds which the Briton is getting on his table every year.
There is a further thought which I should like to give to the house and the country. On the first of January last, the total butter stock on hand in the United States was
42.000. 000 pounds for a population of
130.000.	000. We in Canada had in our warehouses at the same time 22,000,000 pounds for a population of roughly a little over
11.000. 000. In spite of the fact that the United States had only a butter reserve of
42.000.	000 pounds on the first of January last, towards the end of 1942 the United States

The Address-Mr. Blanchette
sent 17,000,000 pounds to relieve conditions in Russia, leaving only 25,000,000 pounds of butter to feed a population of 130,000,000. Here is a blunt fact that we should keep in mind when we attempt to criticize too severely the butter rationing of this country.
Of course the Americans have oleomargarine which they can fall back on, and there has been some agitation in this country, in the press and elsewhere, that we too in Canada should have recourse to oleomargarine to supplement our butter ration. If we do this, then there are only two places where we can get the vegetable oil needed for it, and that is the United States and Great Britain; and once the facts are known, and when we take into consideration also our present Canadian fat allotment of 41 pounds, the same as the allotment in the United States, is there any organization, governmental, commercial or individual, that would have the courage to go to the United States and ask for a share of their vegetable oil, in order that we in Canada might make oleomargarine also? Is there any one in this country who would like to ask Great Britain for a portion of their vegetable oil, with their total quota of 26 pounds of fat, in order that we in Canada might be able to increase our total fats above the 41 pounds which we get at present? I believe, however, that it may be possible for us in Canada to increase our butter production if the wartime prices and trade board would encourage the dairy farmers to produce butter on a larger scale than in the past.
We have heard and are still going to hear a great deal about man-powrer, and I intend to deal with the question as it affects agriculture and lumbering respectively. All the members of this house and the press of the country as well as farming organizations in Canada recognize that there is a shortage of men on the farms. That fact is patent to all who are well versed in the situation, and this beyond any fear or hope of contradiction. If this shortage of man-power on the farms continues, there is no question but that our war effort will be greatly hampered in producing quotas set for the coming year. Agriculture is a primary war industry, equal in importance to the making of munitions and other weapons and engines of war. One is the complement of the other. No country can win a war with munitions alone; both food and munitions are needed for victory.
I have seen it stated editorially in Le Soleil that to-day some 25,000 agricultural workers are in the military camps, and surely these should be returned to the farm, where they belong, in order that the ranks of agricultural workers may be replenished. Recent directions given by the national selective service to the mobilization boards with reference to agricultural workers will greatly help, I hope, not only to maintain on the farms those who remain there, but also to bring back to the farms those who have been taken from them.
In connection with the man-power question, again, some criticism has been made about the permits granted to lumbermen to work across the American border. True it is that last spring some 7,500 men were allowed to go to the United States to work in the lumber-camps near the border, but these permits were gradually cut down periodically. At the time the first permits were granted there was not the shortage of men in the lumber camps that developed later on in the season. Some of the lumber operations to be completed go in cycles, spring and summer, fall and winter, and once we had granted a permit in the spring, it was only logical, as I see it, and in the spirit of the good neighbour, that we should allow these men in limited numbers thereafter, if you wish, to continue to have access to the American lumber camps to complete the lumbering operations in order that the timber cut in the spring and summer would not have to remain and rot in the woods.
Furthermore these men brought badly needed United States exchange to this country, and this on a rather larger scale, since some of the men received $10 to $12 a day for their labour across the border.
I was glad to hear the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) say the other day that the war labour boards had reconsidered 8,500 cases for increase of wages and that as a result 385,000 workers had received in added salary a total of $3,250,000 per month or an annual increase of some $40,000,000. I suggest to him along the same lines a revision of pay for the lumbermen, who are receiving far less than they should. Not everyone can be improvised into a lumberman; it is a trade in itself, one of the most essential in our war effort as well as in peace time, particularly in the reconstruction period to follow the war. All who are cognizant of the situation believe that these men should be paid more for their work. In the province of Quebec I believe the basic rate is $52 a month. Immediately this rate is stated we ask ourselves whether we are doing justice to workers of this class, whose work is seasonal and at times demands endurance of hard conditions of living and hazards and requires courage and skill which should be much better remunerated. And at the same time might it not be advisable to inquire into the price that is being paid for pulp^ in Canada-$13 or $14 for peeled pulp, as compared with $18 and $19 in United

The Address-Mr. Blanchette

States funds for the same product at some of the United States mills of the same hauling distance?
So far as my section is concerned some of these lumber cutting operations consisted in the cutting of veneer logs in the virgin forests, for manufacture of veneers so greatly needed by Great Britain for aircraft production. In allowing these men to cross the border for veneer cutting it was not so much a case of Canada helping the United States as it was the other way round, that the United States were favouring Canada in allowing A-l veneer logs to be cut by Canadians, hauled to Canada, processed in Canadian mills and sent to Britain where there is such dire need for this material. We are receiving neighbourly treatment from the United States in some phases of our war effort, and, as the Minister of Labour put it, we must give some consideration for the favours which we receive.
I have previously stated that some 25,000 agricultural workers are in military camps. I believe that the shortage of men in lumber camps in 1942 was occasioned more by their being called for military service than by the permits granted to work in the lumber camps of the United States. So far as our district of the eastern townships is concerned, when one says agricultural workers one says at the same time labourers for the forests, because these occupations go hand in hand. I have been wondering at times whether it would not be advisable to form a civilian forestry corps composed of workers on the farms, who could very well be employed in the lumber camps during the less active season on the farms. This would at least greatly relieve the shortage of men in the lumber camps.
I now wish to touch upon the matter of social legislation, referred to in' the speech from the throne. I would commend the government in that regard. This government is proceeding in its social legislation in the same manner as the British parliament is approaching the matter, and also to a certain extent the United States government, in that first of all a committee is to be set up to study the measures proposed, after which parliament will be duly seized of the subject and prepared to implement the committee's recommendations. No more far-reaching effect upon this country for many years to come can be had than by the thoroughness and sincerity and activity which the committee created to study this question shall put into its work and agenda and deliberations.
Social legislation is always the most important legislation, and especially is it important at this stage when principles of a

new order have been predicated by the leaders of practically all democratic countries. On June 10, 1941, Right Hon. Arthur Greenwood, minister without portfolio in the British government, announced in the House of Commons that he had arranged with all departments concerned for a comprehensive survey of existing schemes of social insurance and allied services which would be considered in due course by the committee on reconstruction problems of which he was chairman, and that Sir William Beveridge had accepted his invitation to become chairman of an interdepartmental committee which would conduct the survey, giving consideration to representations from representative organizations and persons connected wfith the problem involved.
This report was submitted on November 20, 1942. Social security-the expression used in the Beveridge report-means assurance of a certain income. The plan for social security set out in the report is a plan to win freedom from want by maintaining incomes. But sufficiency of income is not sufficient of itself; freedom from want is only one of the essential freedoms of mankind, and any plan for social security in the narrow sense assumes a concerted social policy in many fields. The plan proposed involves three particular assumptions, namely:	(1) children's allowances; (2) comprehensive health and rehabilitation services; (3) maintenance of employment.
Last session it was my privilege to introduce in this house a resolution based on the principle of family allowances. Like other resolutions of private members it was not called for debate in the house, but it was discussed in some sections of the country and in the press. One of our local papers in an editorial summed up their view in the phrase, "Where is the money to come from?"
At present we are fighting a war unprecedented in the history of the world. Let us make no mistake; we must have recourse to reconstruction, rehabilitation and social reform in a like unprecedented manner after the war. We are spending fabulous sums of money to kill; we must find1 hereafter vast sums to live and let live after the war. The people of the democratic countries are fighting for this very thing at the moment, and will expect nothing less after the war.
In my humble opinion, outstanding as the very keystone of social legislation and reform is the matter of family allowances. This principle was recognized by the British parliament on June 23 last, when the following resolution was proposed and agreed to:

The Address-Mr. White
Resolved, that this house, having regard to the supreme importance of further safeguarding the health and well-being of the rising generation, commends for the immediate consideration of the government the institution of a national scheme of allowances for dependent children as an important contribution to this vital object.
The British House of Commons therefore has recognized that parenthood is both a privilege to the individual and a service to the state.
The case for family allowances rests on the necessity of dealing with three aspects of our national life: first, that we already are within sight of the beginning of a decline in our population; second, that the greatest single factor in poverty is the size of the family; third, the power of the home market to consume the products of industry in the post-war period. When one comes to consider the cost of family allowances it is essential to consider also what will be the cost of going without family allowances. It is not only good social ethics, but looking at it on a lower plane, if you will, it is good business to pay family allowances as has been recommended in the memorandum on reconstruction issued by the Federation of British Industries. A scheme of family allowances is the most efficient single method so far suggested for dealing with social security and poverty, mentioned in the Atlantic charter; by its very nature it offers a master key to social security. Let us not be alarmed by its cost after the war. As a result of the great inventiveness called forth by the war our productive capacity will probably increase rather than diminish when the war is over; for there is a continual increase in the wealth of the country, and it will be frustrated only if we allow men to rot in idleness instead of being absorbed in productive work and in the reconstruction which will be our task after the war.
Should such a scheme be favourably looked upon by the government, and I do not see why it should not, having regard to the favourable outlook in some other countries, I believe we shall be taking a proper step in the right direction of social legislation. By this single measure of family allowances we can solve the most complicated problems of social security and at the same time help along some of the other freedoms which will be the major problems of all governments in the post-war period. Our valiant soldiers are fighting, along with those of our allies, for freedom for themselves and their loved ones, and at the same time for a bill of rights for their children which might be stated as follows: first, the right to healthy childhood; second, the right to education; third, the right to

understand and observe his religious and national heritage; finally, the right to grow up in a world free from the fear of unemployment, insecurity and war.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with many of the previous speakers in this debate who have expressed great satisfaction and pleasure in the turn of the tide in the fortunes of the allied nations, in that they are now passing from the defensive and assuming the offensive. I should like also to compliment the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Booth) on his able and instructive address, which was listened to with great interest by all hon. members, in which he dealt with the work, training and activities of the Canadian troops overseas. In the course of his remarks he paid a fitting and proper tribute to the high esteem in which the officers and men of the Canadian corps are held in Great Britain.
I should like to join also in the regret expressed by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) that there was no mention in the speech from the throne of the heroism and sacrifice of the Canadian boys who went through the Dieppe engagement. In his remarks during the course of this debate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated that in his opinion proper tribute had not been paid in this house to the Canadian boys who fought at Hong Kong. While we in this house may have our differences of opinion as to the sufficiency of the training and equipment of the boys who went to Hong Kong; while there may be some differences of opinion with regard to the Dieppe affair, I am sure there will be no question of division among the people of Canada as to the fighting qualities of and the magnificent battle put up by our boys both at Hong Kong and at Dieppe. These two names will long be remembered in Canada. When one considers the almost impossible odds against which our boys battled at Hong Kong; when one considers the enemy, vastly superior in numbers, highly trained and. fully equipped, one can ' only feel a great thrill of pride at the achievements of the Canadian boys, followed by a grim resolve that those boys must and will be avenged. And who among us here can picture the beachhead at Dieppe on that summer morning when the Canadian troops stormed ashore against the hail of death that was hurled upon them? Yet all the press dispatches and articles written by men who were there indicate that not a single man faltered in his task. The boys who made up those contingents at Dieppe and Hong Kong came from communities right across this
The Address-Mr. White

whole dominion, and I am sure that tomorrow, when the historian records with unprejudiced pen the events of these historic days, the names of Hong Kong and Dieppe, together with the names of the officers and men who fought there, will be placed high on the Canadian scroll of honour.
Previous speakers have dealt with certain matters relating to lumbering and farming in various parts of Canada, and I should like to deal briefly with these same subjects, because they concern the part of Ontario in which I reside. In the counties of Peterborough and Hastings there are almost inexhaustible supplies of wood and a certain quantity of timber. For many years the wood and lumber industry has provided a livelihood for a large number of persons. During the winter of 1941-42 many wood operators, both individuals and companies, took out large quantities of fuel wood for sale during the fall of 1942 and this present winter. At that time there was no price ceiling on wood. On August 8, 1942, however, a price ceiling was imposed, providing a certain price at roadside and a certain price for the delivered dry wood. Owing to a scarcity of other fuels throughout the dominion this large supply of wood was soon sold at ceiling prices. The price set by the fuel administrator resulted in a loss, in many instances, for the individual or wood operator.
After, the wood was sold, after there had been many complaints and after the wood controller discovered that he had set the price of wood too low, early in January 1943 the price was increased by $2 a cord. This increase to the wood operator just meant the difference between operating at a loss and breaking even or having a fair profit. Hon. members would be interested to know who advised the fuel administrator when he set the price on fuel wood, because I am sure any hon. member who lives in a district in which there are dealings in wood must agree with me when I say that the price of fuel wood, either at roadside or delivered, as set by the fuel controller in his order of August, 1942, was too low. While the price was raised, the increase was made too late in the season. January of this year was too late for any wood operator or company to make contracts or arrangements to take out wood during the present winter. Up to that date they were faced with a low fixed price. The wood operator had to make a bargain with the owner of the wood lot. He had to make provision for the cutting of the wood, for the trucking of it from the wood lot to the roadside, and the piling at that point. He had to arrange with the trucker who would pick up the wood at the roadside and make 
deliveries to consumers in towns, villages or cities. Naturally any man who owned a wood lot wanted a fair price for his wood; the workman wanted a fair price, the trucker wanted a fair price-they all wanted a fair price, and they were entitled to it. The result has been that this winter in the counties of Hastings and Peterborough no one is taking out any wood or making provision for the sale of wood during the next winter season. This situation will become more serious, because these counties supply not only many small towns and villages, but also several large cities in the immediate vicinity.
Next comes the question of labour. No provision has yet been made under which the lumber or wood dealer can obtain a proper supply of labour to carry out his operations. The same condition applies to the lumber industry in my district. Lumber operators in the counties of Hastings and Peterborough might properly be classed as small operators, because they take out a cut of only half a million to two million feet a year. In addition they supply poles, ties and material of the kind.
During the summer of 1942 I had occasion to apply to the divisional registrar for the exemption from or postponement of service of a young man who was a lumber sawyer. This young man had been called for military service, and had been granted one or two exemptions, following which he had received his final notice to report. As the calling of sawyers and other key men in the lumber industry affected many in the counties of Hastings and Peterborough, I prepared a short brief dealing with the labour and lumber situation as it applied in my community, and I attended with the young man before the board at Kingston. After consulting with the board, however, the registrar advised me that as I was a lawyer I could not appear before the board or submit my brief. I then asked the registrar if I could appear as a member of parliament, and after a second consultation with the board he advised me I could not. However the young man was allowed to appear and state his case before the board, at which there was present an officer in uniform. He was refused any further exemption; but the registrar did mention one thing to me, namely that the small lumber operator for whom this sawyer was working did not have any government contract. That was true; very few small lumber operators have government contracts. But the fact remains that practically all the lumber, poles, timber and ties they take out are sold to industrial plants which are working on

The Address-Mr. White
government contracts. The operator in question had a large contract to supply lumber to the cement company at Pointe Anne, and he was supplying all the timber he could get of a certain kind to the shipyards at Kingston.
Just a few days after my visit to Kingston I received from the timber controller a long document dated September 1, 1942, which, I believe, all hon. members received. This document, addressed to Canada's lumber industry, states in the first paragraph:
The paramount thing at the present time in the national interest is the maximum production of logs and lumber. We must accomplish this, even with our present difficulties of labour shortage,-
And so on.
Then follows a long list of districts in which lumbering is carried on. I wrote the timber controller and Mr. Little, who was then in charge of selective service, setting out the case of the wood and lumber operators in my counties. As usual I received a courteous reply from the director of national selective service, and a similar letter from the timber controller. In their letters they both pointed out that the matter of exemption of key men in the lumber industry had been brought to their attention before, that something was going to be worked out, that it was necessary that lumber be produced-and all the rest of it,-and that I would be advised in due course of what further action would be taken. That was the last I heard of the matter.
In closing this part of my observations may I point out that while these lumber operators are small, they have fairly large investments in equipment and machinery. They are all ready to operate. The government is urging that our lumber production be increased. With a set-up like this it seems most unfortunate that key men in the industry should be called for military service, and it is also unfortunate that the lumber operators are not permitted to obtain adequate labour to carry on this most important industry.
With respect to farm labour in my constituency I would point out that in 1942 the county of Hastings held the record for the largest cheese and pork products production in Ontario. The farmers have been asked to increase their pork production in 1943 by twenty per cent, and to increase further their cheese production, which is already at a record. There are in addition in these two counties many creameries which make anywhere from 200,000 to 700,000 pounds or more of butter a year. They also raise large quantities of beef, lamb, poultry, honey and other farm products. These two counties are
ideally suited for mixed farming. I know all members will agree with me when I say that the farmer is just as willing and anxious as anyone else to produce the maximum amount for the war effort, but like the lumber dealer or the wood operator he is faced with a shortage of help. Large numbers of men in these two counties have enlisted in the armed forces, and large numbers of men and women have gone into the industrial centres. Many of our young men also have been called for military service. The result is that to-day on many farms you will find a farmer with only his wife to assist him in operating a farm which in normal times would have at least two or three men. If the farmer is to increase his production as he has been asked to do in 1943 he must be able to plan at least one season ahead; for he must increase his stock and arrange to cultivate a larger area in order to grow more feed.
As hon. members know, there is no such thing under the war service regulations as a permanent exemption. Postponements are granted which are renewable from time to time, or a man may receive a postponement until further notice. I know many young men in my district who received their callup notice together with a transport warrant and instructions to report at the district depot in a matter of three or four days. It was a sorry spectacle last fall, Mr. Speaker, to see many crops of hay and grain left to rot in the snow simply because of the shortage of farm help. I would point out to the minister that the notices that are sent out to the young men by registered mail, enclosing a transport warrant and instructions to report at a depot, reach the young men in the country only two or three days before they are directed to report at the district depot. A sufficient time is not allowed to them to make application for .postponement. I have been told that when the young man goes to the district depot and has been medically examined and accepted he is then allowed to apply for a postponement, but there is nothing in the call-up notice itself to indicate that he is entitled to apply for postponement at the district depot. The result has been that many of our young men from the farms, once they got to the district depot and passed the medical officer, soon found themselves in uniform.
The average farmer engaged in mixed farming, like the lumber or wood operator, for instance, has a large investment in his operations, and when his farm help is taken away he has no alternative but to reduce his stock and to cut down the number of acres he has under cultivation.
The Address-Mr. White

In the booklet, "Canada at War" No. 19, for December, 1942, it is stated at page 3 that in the army in Canada there are approximately
210.000	troops on active service, in addition to 200,000 men in the reserve army. It does not state in the book whether the figure of
210.000	troops on active service in Canada includes young men who have been called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act. I trust that when the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) speaks he will inform the house how this figure of 210,000 is made up, and whether it includes the "R" recruits. On the next page of the book it is stated that there are overseas upwards of
180.000	men, comprising five divisions.
Other members in referring to the troops
overseas have brought up the important question whether adequate reinforcements have been provided. I would ask the Minister of National Defence, when he speaks on this important question of reinforcements, not to confine himself to simply stating that there are "adequate" reinforcements or some adjective of the kind. I ask him to tell us what percentage of reinforcements are needed, what percentage basis has been worked out. If the percentage basis is five, ten, twenty, or fifty per cent, I for one should like to know. I have inquired of many officers and I have never yet been able to find out the basis of what are considered adequate reinforcements. As was pointed out very forcefully by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) yesterday, at Dieppe our casualties were some sixty-seven per cent. It is most important that the minister should tell us frankly the percentage basis of our reinforcements. I hope that he will be able to assure the house that no matter what type of action the Canadian forces may be engaged in overseas, provision has been made for supplying them with the necessary reinforcements to maintain the army as constituted at present.
In the next issue of "Canada at War", for January, an interesting table is given on page 20, showing the enlistments in the three branches of -the armed forces. This table has been reproduced in the press and has caused much comment in various editorials. The table clearly shows that some sections of the country are supplying many more recruits than other sections. The table also shows the number of recruits who enlisted in the war of 1914-18, but whoever prepared the table neglected to show the approximate population of Canada in 1914 and its approximate population in 1939; nor does this table show the approximate number of discharges or casualties to date.

The book also states that there are 200,000 men in our reserve army. I would ask the Minister of National Defence when he speaks to say whether that 200,000 is only a paper estimate, and to tell us how many men in the reserve army are actually training. The minister might further explain why it is necessary to keep an army of 210,000 men in Canada, because under recent regulations married men between certain ages are being called for military training, and regulations were recently passed providing that boys of seventeen years of age can be accepted in the armed forces. I ask the Minister of National Defence how he can possibly justify the accepting of boys seventeen years of age in the armed forces; because if a lad of that age takes the basic training, it lasts only two months; if he takes his advanced training, that is a further two months; and if he takes a course at a trade school, for instance, I understand it requires not more than seven to nine months, so that he still has some eleven months to put in before he can proceed overseas.
Perhaps this calling up of the married men and the accepting in the army of boys of seventeen is just another example of the effort to swell enlistment figures; or is it another example of trying to dodge the issue or delay the day when compulsory selective service for anywhere in the world will be put into effect? I for one would like to have the Minister of National Defence, when he speaks, explain fully why it is necessary to take boys of seventeen years of age into the armed forces.
The Prime Minister, as reported in Hansard, page 46, made this remark:	*
Little if any account has been taken of the fact that unless there had been very careful planning at the outset, all the rest might likely have been a muddle. I claim for the present administration that we have planned carefully from the start.
Let me review briefly the "careful planning" which has taken place in regard to obtaining recruits for the armed forces.
In 1940 there was passed, with a great blare of trumpets, the National Resources Mobilization Act. But after parliament went home, regulations were passed by order in council which restricted the training to thirty days. Public opinion soon realized what a farce this thirty-day training was, and demanded a change, and it was changed to four months. Public opinion developed further, and it was then changed to "service for the duration", but subject always to the restriction that these men could1 not serve outside Canada. Again public opinion forced the government to take some action, and we had the second farce of the plebiscite which caused months

The Address-Mr. White
of further delay. After the plebiscite, which resulted in a large vote in favour of releasing the government from its promise, we had an amendment to the act, but this was nullified by the fact that it was not .put into force, and is still not in operation. Does the Prime Minister pretend to claim that there was careful planning in regard to this matter? Can, he dispute the fact that the whole operation of the act has been a muddle all the way through?
Then we have the question of the very large number of notices sent out, totalling some 750,611, requiring young men to report. Of this number, 146,276 were classed as delinquents or otherwise unaccounted for, some 96,830 notices were not delivered, and after it was all boiled down the mobilization machinery only got into the army some 14-3 per cent of the men who were called up. Does that look like careful planning to prevent a muddle?
Then we have the Hong Kong affair. Does anybody pretend to say that it was carefully planned and that there was no muddle? One has only to read the many dispatches in the press as to the training of the boys and the nature of the equipment they had at Dieppe, and compare that with the nature of the training and the equipment the boys had at Hong Kong, to see whether or not there was any kind of muddle.
Does the Prime Minister think there was very careful planning in the man-power situation which was so well reviewed yesterday by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), in which he set out the different changes, the new regulations which were passed every two or three months? Even during this debate, practically every speaker, irrespective of the party to which he belongs, has pointed out the very serious man-power situation. I wonder whether the Prime Minister thinks there was very careful planning in regard to that.
The Minister of Labour is not in his seat, but I wonder what he would say to this statement. Does he think there was very careful planning and no muddle as regards his labour policy? Is not the labour policy of this government responsible for the present unrest in labour and for the very recent steel and other strikes?
Then we have the question of cost of living bonuses for members of the armed forces. Was there any muddle about that? They are the one class of men and women who should have been the very first to receive the cost of living bonus, but instead of being the first they were the last, and they received it only after the greatest public pressure.
There is also the question of the various registrations which have taken place in this country, commencing with the national registration of 1940 and continuing down to date. Has that been a muddle? It has been a muddle from the very start, and I am advised that it is going to be necessary to have another registration before it can be straightened out.
Time does not permit me to deal with the social security legislation, but I should like to mention and to concur in a remark made by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Mayhew), on February 15, when, speaking of returned soldiers, he said.-Hansard, page 441:
I think we have reached the time when the onus of proving that a man's health has been impaired, that he has contracted tuberculosis on account of service overseas, should be the other way around; that the government should have to prove to the soldier that he did not contract the disease while away.
The hon. member who made that statement has put his finger on one of the most objectionable features of the whole pensions administration. Why should it be necessary for any soldier to have to go to his member of parliament, or to his mayor, or to a lawyer or anybody else to take up his case with the pensions board? Why should any private soldier have to fight the endless red tape of the pensions board? I know the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) will probably dispute that; but after some twenty years' experience in handling cases before the pensions board I have a pretty good idea of how tough they are to deal with. As I said once before in this house, if they would have on the administration boards of the pensions commission a few men who actually served overseas as privates, much of the present hardship would disappear.
Much has been said about the treatment handed out to the soldier who has been discharged in this war. If this government cannot ensure freedom from want to the small number of soldiers who have been discharged, how in the world do they expect to bring in a programme which will care for hundreds of thousands of persons after the war? The citizens of Canada do not want ex-service men cast aside with a small pension and obliged to tramp the streets looking for work. In my opinion the rehabilitation and care of the exservice men is the most important job facing this parliament and the people of Canada. There should be proper plans and programmes of care for them, to see that they obtain gainful employment as soon as they are able to go to work.
The Address-Mr. White

In conclusion, there are several points which I should like to emphasize and lay before the government:
1.	That the government consider the appointment of a minister to deal solely with soldiers' problems.
2.	That the government produce to parliament the complete report of the Hong Kong investigation.
3.	That a proper adjustment be made in farm prices.
4.	That proper provision be made for the supply of adequate labour for farmers, wood and lumber dealers.
5.	That the amendment to the National Resources Mobilization Act passed at the last session be brought into force at once so that all members of the armed forces will be available for service anywhere in the world.
6.	That the government arrange in the near future for a secret session of this house when the Prime Minister may give the members a complete report of the Casablanca conference, and a complete report on the political situation in North Africa; that the Minister of National Defence may give a complete statement on our forces overseas and the matter of reinforcements; that private members may have the opportunity of asking the three defence ministers questions relating to the armed forces that cannot be asked in the house at a public sitting; and that the Minister of National Defence make a statement on the Dieppe operation.
7.	That the government consider the granting of commissions to all aircrew overseas.
8.	That the government introduce at this session, legislation along the lines of the Sparkman Act and the Soldiers' and Sailors' Civil Relief Act as passed by the United States congress to cover the following in regard to members of the armed forces:
(a)	No eviction of families of those in service.
(b)	No foreclosure of mortgage during period of service or for a reasonable period after the end of the war.
(c)	No seizure or foreclosure of property for taxes.
(d)	No forfeiture of instalment contracts except where things purchased are of a wasting character.
(e)	Protection of life insurance policies against cancellation for non-payment of premiums.
(f)	Protection against judgment or other legal proceedings for debts incurred before enlistment or call.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The speech from the throne of this session contains a statement concerning our improved position in the war, but at the same time it cautions us not to become overoptimistic lest we slacken in our war effort. Rather it suggests that we should increase our effort to attain our objective more quickly and with complete decisiveness. Among other things, the speech also provides a basis for the discussion of post-war reconstruction. So far in this debate many aspects of this latter item have already been dealt with by hon. members on both sides of the house. Speakers have particularly emphasized certain phases of social and economic problems. I should like, therefore, to add to this discussion by considering what I believe to be other important phases of the subject of post-war reconstruction, namely, Canada's relationship to the British commonwealth of nations, and Canada's nationhood in the post-war world.
I believe it will be generally conceded that the present struggle is more of a revolution than merely a war. It is definitely a struggle of ideologies. It is a struggle of philosophies of life. It is a struggle of peoples and powers. But more definitely than that, it is a struggle of the sovereignty of the individual within a sovereign nation as against the onrush of totalitarianism in one form or another.
There are, in my opinion, two main features of this revolutionary war. The one is that of its global or international character; the other is that of a domestic or national character. On the international scale it touches the structures upon which is based the relationship of many peoples and many powers to one another, while on the national scale it embraces the underlying principles of our social, economic and political aspects of life. This titanic eruption is the natural outcome of the unnatural shape of things of pre-war days. We realize now that we are forced to fight not only the axis powers, but also many evils of our own creation-our own mistakes, and our own blunders. We also know that we are paying a high price for these mistakes, in human life and in suffering. Therefore we dare not repeat them in the future.	_
Again, our present position may be likened to that of a ship on a stormy sea. On our hazardous journey we find ourselves in the midst of cross-currents and undercurrents of fascism, nazism, federal unionism and many other forms of "isms" which are out to destroy sovereignty-the very basis of democracy- the ideal which stands for the maximum amount of individual and national freedom.

The Address-Mr. Hlynka
In view of this fact we must guard against the possibility of being swept away by some of these currents and finding ourselves after the war with an ideology totally foreign to our Canadian way of life. Therefore it is imperative that we apply ourselves most vigorously to the task of liquidating the many obstacles which have stood between the people and their social, economic and political security. But at the same time we must exercise great care not to lose the positive accomplishments which we have evolved over the centuries. Among these accomplishments I list Canada's position within the British commonwealth of nations. This I wish to discuss now.
To me the British crown is the heart and symbol of the British commonwealth of free and sovereign peoples. To me the British crown is the symbol of unity and the heritage of British ideals of more than a thousand years. More than that, we should prize our position within the commonwealth because we are the benefactors in all and everything that has been achieved over centuries of progress. For instance, should it not occur to us that we are equal partners in a unique association of free sovereign nations, created by an orderly process of evolution in practical statecraft? Let me point out the underlying principle of our British democratic system. It is simply this, that the extent and the power of the British commonwealth of nations are consistent with the maximum of individual freedom, the maximum of local and provincial autonomy, and the maximum of sovereignty of each unit-nation, fitting into the pattern of the commonwealth. This philosophy of statecraft has been built on practical experience, and it is opposed to other philosophies which are supported by many, and which include the surrender of our national sovereignty in favour of some superstate. It will further be apparent from this comparison that the philosophy of the British people is diametrically opposite to that of totalitarianism in whatever form it appears.
In addition to what I have already said about the British commonwealth of nations we should also keep constantly in mind the fact that it was the British commonwealth of nations, and particularly the heroic British, who stood alone after the fall of France and single-handed saved the world from totalitarianism while others hesitatingly speculated. Therefore irrespective of what victories the allies have won so far and irrespective of what victories we shall win in the future, the credit for the greatest role in our total victory should undoubtedly go to the British. It is my 72537-34
definite conviction that democracy' will live so long as the British commonwealth of nations lives, and that Canada will remain Canada so long as we share our heritage and our responsibilities with the British commonwealth of nations. Therefore I repeat that however close our association and our cooperation with other nations shall be in the future, the road of Canada is the road of the British commonwealth of nations.
So far I have dealt briefly with only a few of the outstanding features of our British heritage which we must retain from the past and the present and which must be projected into the future of post-war reconstruction. In addition we have acquired an equally priceless heritage in our own national life. The experiences of our forefathers which crystallized into self-government must not now be discarded, under the terrific impact of events, in favour of some system based on the surrender of our national sovereignty. The integrity of Canada's nationhood must forever remain our guiding principle. Therefore I should like now to (Jiscuss briefly our nationhood.
Speaking before the Canadian Institute of International Affairs in October, 1937, Lord Tweedsmuir, a great Britisher and an equally great Canadian, made the following statement:
She (Canada) is a sovereign nation and cannot take her attitude to the world docilely from Britain or from the United States or from anybody else. A Canadian's first loyalty is not to the British commonwealth of nations, but to Canada and to Canada's king, and those who deny this are doing, to my mind, a great disservice to the commonwealth.
This statement, sir, expresses my sentiments on the subject. Therefore keeping in mind what I said in the first part of my address, that I do not care to subscribe to any "isms" of a social or political order, I wish to say, however, that I am a strong believer in one "ism" and that is Canadianism. It is my sincere conviction that if Canada is to make her utmost contribution to the winning of the war, and if she is to take her rightful place in the council of the nations, she must assume the role of a fully self-governing nation both in national and in international affairs.
Constitutionally Canada is now a sovereign nation, and also a self-governing nation. At the same time she is an equal partner in the commonwealth. This status was conferred upon Canada by the statute of Westminster, passed in 1931. Therefore Canada, having acquired this national maturity, now stands on the threshold of a new era.
While it must be admitted that certain changes and certain adjustments of a constitutional or legal nature must still be made, the

The Address-Mr. Hlynka

chief obstacles in the way of realization of our full nationhood lie, in the main, in the cultural and economic spheres. Although we have drawn upon Great Britain for much of what we possess in the way of culture, traditions, history, our way of life, our institutions, and centuries of experience in practical statecraft, nevertheless we have now arrived at a stage where we must begin to develop our own distinctive character.
I have already made reference to the constitutional and political framework of our nation. We also have a territory broad in extent and rich in natural resources. The third important element in the making of a nation is its people. We have drawn for our citizenship upon people of many nationalities, with rich and varied backgrounds. This diversity should by no means be a source of weakness; rather it should be a source of strength and potential cultural wealth. Here again is a task for the government, to bring about a harmonious coordination of these varied cultures into our common Canadian mosaic. Polite tolerance toward citizens of varied ethnic backgrounds is not enough; we must oifer them something more positive. We must once and for all time realize that Johnson and Ivanyshyn are equally genuine Canadian names; for they mean one and the same thing. After all, the casualty lists of Dieppe did not draw any such distinctions.
So that when we undertake the task of postwar reconstruction in Canada we must do more than attain an outward unity; this unity must find expression in a common Canadian culture and a common Canadian spirit. While we are undertaking this whole development of our Canadian nationhood we must also keep in mind the fact that this development is necessarily based on the degree of economic welfare of our people. This should not be an obstacle in Canada's way, because we are the owners of one of the richest territories in the world. We have the capacity to produce more than we need, and of all sorts of commodities for all our people. . One of our main obstacles in the past has been our inability to distribute our products and the unwillingness of governments to tackle this problem in a modern, scientific manner. I believe, however, that the time is not too far distant when it will be considered criminal mismanagement of the affairs of the people to permit goods and services to lie dormant while people starve in need of them.
I have made only a brief statement, Mr. Speaker, in approaching this great problem. I have tried to point out at least a few of the things that we must retain from our way of

life, and at the same time I have made an endeavour to indicate some of the things which must be added. Should we fail in this task, as we failed in the past, we will be exposing ourselves, on the home front, to the danger of losing ground to totalitarianism in spite of our victories on the field of battle.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a tendency in Canada today, and even in this house, to consider that the war is already won. I think this is deplorable. It is, however, the natural consequence of the government's policy of easing us gently into total war. For us in Canada it may reasonably be said that the decisive fighting still lies ahead. Because it is dangerous to look upon the war as already won there is no reason why we should not consider briefly the methods of winning it and the pattern of hostilities from now until the collapse of Germany.
I think it is reasonable to assume that we will be attacking Hitler's so-called fortress of Europe with our land forces in the reasonably near future. That the Canadian army will fight with the traditional heroism and fortitude of the Canadian expeditionary force of the last war goes without saying. It is unfortunate but also inevitable that casualties will be suffered at a rate even greater than during the first world war. I do not wish to take Dieppe as an example, but it must be remembered that there we suffered casualties amounting to almost seventy per cent of our effectives in a period of a little over nine hours. There is no military operation so hazardous as attacking, over a considerable body of water, a well-fortified shore base.
I have made these statements and brought out these unpleasant facts merely to lead up to the man-power situation in Canada. I do not know precisely the situation with regard to our trained reinforcements overseas. I believe, however, that they are insufficient to maintain the Canadian army at striking-force, shock-troop efficiency for an intensive campaign of even medium duration. It is therefore probable that the powers given to the government in the plebiscite may have to be invoked, and that soldiers in the home defence army may have to be sent outside of Canada as reinforcements for our troops fighting against Hitler. In mentioning this I make the plea to the government that when this decision has to be taken they do not call a snap election in order to obtain further authority from the people. To call an election during these intensive operations would be nothing short of infamous.

The Address-Mr. Adamson
The other night the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) quoted at length the message from General McNaughton to the troops on New Year's day, 1943. Dealing with the arrival of the first Canadian contingent overseas General McNaughton said:
At that time our numbers of trained soldiers and experienced officers were very few indeed and our equipment consisted of little more than the rifles we carried and the clothing we wore.
I should like to compare that statement with a speech made by the then Minister of Finance, the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) at Kingston on March 8, 1940, during the heat of an election campaign. I quote from the Ottawa Evening Citizen of March 9, 1940; these are the headlines:
Ralston Says Canadians Went Over With Own Artillery, Machine Guns. Finance Minister Says Full Equipment Carried. Makes Known for First Time that Contingents Well Armed Before Proceeding Overseas.
The whole trend of the article gives the impression that the first Canadian division landed in England well equipped and ready for action. If a snap election is called, this is the sort of thing we may expect. With every day and every hour of vital importance we will see ministers going around the country campaigning, while the whole business of government will be aborted. The government now has all the authority in connection with man-power it can possibly need. It must be prepared to use it.
I come now, Mr. Speaker, to a subject second only in importance to that of the war; namely, the definite danger of inflation. What I am about to say will no doubt be unpopular with certain sections of the people, since there is no drug, no stimulating intoxicant, as wholly delightful as inflation in its early stages. It is easy to make sectional appeals and invite strife in both primary and secondary industries which would tend to break the price ceiling. In many cases the fantastic stupidity of controllers has caused derision and bungling. The regulations frequently defeat their own ends. They are ill-advised, hurriedly built bits of legislation which, because the government does not trust this house, have been imposed upon the Canadian people. Notwithstanding what I have said, however, I believe we must do everything we can to maintain the price structure on as even a keel as possible.
There is no reason for those who would like to see inflation to worry. No matter what controls either this government or the government of the United States imposes we are in an inflationary cycle which may, unless we are extremely careful, bring disaster. I see by the 72537-34J
press to-day that we are spending at the rate of over five billion dollars a year. We are raising by taxation a little over two billions. The United States is spending close to eight billion dollars a month, and raising by taxation approximately two billions. That should give us sufficient warning. At present, particularly in the United States, reliance is placed on the desire of the people to invest or hoard their money. If this tendency shows signs of decreasing the strain on the price level of basic commodities may result in a fearsomely quick spiral of inflation.
As an illustration of what I mean when I speak of a condition where there is no control let me give a few examples of prices in England. These figures are for uncontrolled articles, or articles which in some cases may be considered luxuries. They do however give some indication of what people will pay, and what can happen to a price structure if the control is broken. These are not black market prices, but prices I saw for myself in London in the fall of 1942, just a few months ago. Here are a few of them: An ear of corn, 75 cents; a peach, $2.10; a bunch of grapes, $6; a bottle of brandy-purchased at an auction sale at Christie's-$48, a dozen oysters. $7.50. I could give a longer list, but were I to do so I might have to use proprietary names, and I would rather avoid doing that.
Our present situation is illustrated by an incident I observed when I was overseas. A Focke-Wulf 190 had come over, making a hit-and-run raid on a town in the southeast of England. As in many of such raids, it tackled the biggest thing it saw, which on that occasion happened to be the town gasometer-a large round tank about eighty feet high, full of coal gas for domestic purposes. It shot the gas holder full of holes, both with cannon and with machine guns. From each of the holes little spurts of flame were shooting into the air. On the top of the gas holder two employees of the gas company were courageously running around with sand bags, and every time a spurt of flame appeared it would be covered by a sand bag. Meantime other sand bags were being hauled up from the ground. I happened to be passing by with an air force officer, and I said to him, " What a terrific spectacle it would be if the thing went up." He said to me, " Yes, but neither you nor I would be here to see it." Incidentally, I might add that subsequently both the employees to whom I have referred were decorated for valour.
This incident is to me a symbol of what is happening in Canada to-day. We have certain necessary controls on price structure. People -unthinkingly, I believe-are doing every-
The Address-Mr. Adamson

thing they can to break them wherever they can. I believe we should do everything in our power to assist the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) in his very difficult job of maintaining the country on an even economic balance.
For a time I lived in a country in South America where, in a period of a little less than three months the value of the currency decreased by sixty-five per cent. This, of course, was not the wild inflation of Germany; but I have not forgotten the scenes of hardship suffered by the native population. May I suggest in passing that hon. members who are interested in the subject would do well to read an article by Doctor Palyi, who was an official of the Reichsbank. This article appeared in the Northern Miner of February 4. I believe that completes all I have to say on the subject of inflation.
1 now come to what might be called shelter, because to grace the present living conditions in many parts of our urban centres with the term housing would be wrong. We must look closely and dispassionately on the conditions which now exist, and also on the contributory causes which made those conditions. Furthermore we must be fearless in our approach to the subject, and prescribe and carry out the cure. Naturally it is impossible for a layman like myself adequately to cover so vast a subject. There are people in Canada who are experts and who, I hope, will be called before the committee on reconstruction at this session.
Let us, however, look very generally at the situation as it exists. Before the war the average yearly construction of new houses was 15,000. The need was 65,000. It has been estimated that there was a backlog of needed houses amounting to 150,000, across Canada,
110,000	of which existed in urban communities of over 30,000 population. It is obvious that the situation has become much more acute during the war years-and this despite all the efforts of Wartime Housing Limited. It has further been estimated in Washington, officially, by Frederick M. Babcock, that Canada must build in the ten-year period subsequent to the war between 750,000 and a million houses, in order to maintain a reasonable standard of living. Under the Canadian economy before the war sixty per cent of the population were unable to buy what the market afforded. This is based on the established theory that twenty per cent of the gross income of a family should go for shelter. The cost of production per house by private enterprise is too high to satisfy the needs of sixty per cent of the population. When I refer to housing I mean decent
IMr. Adamson.]
houses-not the substandard dwelling so common in our urban communities. It has been estimated that the income of fifty per cent of our population is less than $1,000 a year, and ten per cent have actually less than $600 a year. On the basis of twenty per cent of their income for shelter they could afford to pay only $10 to $17 a month for rent. It is obvious they cannot get shelter for anything like this sum, so that they pay more and go without their full quota of one or other of the essentials of life, such as proper food, clothing or medical care.
There is material available to show the effect that slums produced by these conditions have on Canadians. There is infinitely more material available concerning such conditions in the United States. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I shall quote briefly from a few typical reports, and first from a report submitted to the Toronto board of control by a committee on housing in that city. The report was submitted in November, 1942, and this is what it has to say in the first paragraph about health:
Many people are living under conditions which are injurious to health.
This is 1942, remember! It goes on:
In certain areas men, women and children are existing in basements designed for vegetable or other storage; others are housed in damp, cold, draughty and vermin-infested quarters; as many as eight persons are living, eating and sleeping in one room. Evictions and threats of eviction are putting a heavy strain on the physical and moral reserves of soldiers' dependents, war workers and persons in the low income group, in fact on all who are unable to purchase houses or to find suitable rentable accommodation.
It goes on to give figures comparing the health standards in two areas of the city, Yorkville and Moss Park, but these figures have been quoted so frequently that I shall not put them on Hansard. They can be found in the brief submitted by the federation of agriculture, in Health, and in many other publications.
I should like to quote from the Journal of the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada, from a report on housing made by Professor E. R. Arthur, of the university of Toronto, in September, 1942. Professor Arthur says- I shall quote just two paragraphs:
The lieutenant-governor's report on housing conditions in Toronto published in 1934 first drew the attention of the general public to the fact that a Canadian city housed a large section of its citizens in conditions not much higher than would be demanded for animals. Of 1,339 dwellings examined, 43 per cent were without cellars, 82 per cent had no method of heating other than stoves, 58 per cent were damp and 20 per cent subject to flood; 55 per cent were verminous, 59 per cent were without baths and

The Address-Mr. Adamson
20 per cent had outside toilets subject to freezing. The houses examined are in a great slum area which we still have. Since 1934 a committee of civil officials has condemned some houses and enforced the repairs and improvements of others. The condemnation of houses has aggravated congestion in an area, where in 1934, 57 per cent averaged more than one person per room and 16 per cent averaged two or more persons per room. "Improvement" has kept the inhabitants of some dwellings dry, but the congestion remains the same or worse, and the environment grows progressively undesirable. The lieutenant-governor's report caused a mild stir and had the effect of bandaging a gangrenous sore where an operation of a major character was necessary.
