speechtext:
Notwithstanding the pleasant remark of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) the other day, with reference to my two colleagues, the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Lacroix), and the hon. member for Beauharnois-La-prairie (Mr. Raymond), and myself, I am not ashamed to address this house from an opposition bench. For the first time after having attended sixteen sessions of parliament I am opposing a government. Had the Liberal party fulfilled its engagement and honoured its word, I would not be here. The delegation of Quebec has been sworn in, especially during the provincial election of 1939, before the people of the province, that "no one would support any government, be it Liberal or Conservative, and every one would oppose any government that would vote for conscription for overseas, or apply it". This was our oath. No one should forget it now that conscription has been voted by a Liberal government and, whatever can be said, is applied. No one here should be surprised to see us on this side of the house. The present conscription differs in its application from the conscription of 1917, but it is working perfectly.
May I be permitted to give a few examples. Take, for instance, a member of this house giving a recommendation in favour of a married man, let us say, thirty years of age, with a wife and three children. This man cannot be appointed as postmaster if he is of military age, and if he has no discharge from military service. The result is this: no discharge, no position; no position, no meals, no clothing. A man thirty-seven years of age with a wife and seven children applied for a position as blacksmith in the marine department in Quebec. The first question was, Since you are of military age. have you been discharged from the army? The result is: no discharge from the army, no job. Since these two men could not enlist voluntarily for home defence, but could enlist voluntarily only in the active forces, because they were not called up in accordance with the National Resources Mobilization Act, they are free to enlist for overseas or to remain without a job. No job, no meals, no clothing, no living. Let us examine the case of a young doctor, single or married, but without children, aged twenty-five. Under the act, he is called up for military service. He enjoys perfect freedom with respect to military service. If he wants to serve as a medical man in the army, he must enlist in the active forces to serve anywhere in the world; otherwise he must serve as a private in home defence. A wonderful voluntary system! Take the case of a young student in one of the last two years of his

The Address-Mr. Gauthier
classical course. Success does not always smile on the most brilliant pupils, and if this young man is unfortunate enough to fail, he is not given another chance to go through. The road is wide open before him to the army. A consoling voluntary system!
As a resume of all this, I would say, as one of my * friends said one day, this is a real voluntary system: you do not want to enlist but the government wants you to, and there you are. These are a few cases of the newly patented voluntary system for the recruiting of Canadian soldiers for overseas in the second world war.
Under the authority of order in council P.C. 11159, Canadian soldiers have been sent to Newfoundland, Alaska and Labrador. Another step further. The next is overseas; and if there is another delay between the promised order in council and the divulging of it, our soldiers will have time to write to their parents and receive an answer before the government has decided to make the order in council public. A very open and frank policy! The coating used by the politicians of the two old political parties of this country has become too thin, so thin that the people taste the pill and refuse to swallow it. The policy ends at the same spot; the ways of application differ.
The war effort was too inadequate, the government) too slow for our Conservative friends, and by studied and well organized pressure they have forced the Liberals to come across. These promises of a moderate and voluntary effort to win the provincial elections of 1939 in Quebec have volatilized under the warm rays of the imperial sun and the cacophonic brass band of the two hundred. An identical offensive on the plebiscite put into action the old see-saw policy invented to conciliate finance, the politicians and the claims of the people.
We witnessed in this house strongly opposed members voting in favour of the plebiscite, and it has been admitted by members sitting in this house and by many newspapers that an important percentage of the population did not exactly know whether this "yes" or "no" vote was connected with conscription. It had been so clearly put before the people! However, one thing certain is that the "no" vote in Quebec was against conscription and, if it has changed, it is toward an increase in the negative vote. It was then that a new word was bom, a word that is now used freely with reference to those who are opposing the old political parties in this country-"isolationist." What a handy word! For a few years the word "communist" had been stewed on every occasion where the old political parties wanted
to stigmatize their opponents, especially those strongly advocating reforms on social and economic grounds, and in accordance with a true Canadian policy. Now, however, that Mr. Buck and his partisans, members of a party which has not yet been legalized, can spread vigorous propaganda everywhere in the country; now that help to Russia has become a duty among the united nations; now that Russia itself has balanced the fortunes of war in our favour, the word "communist" does not fit any longer. "Isolationist" is the new blend.
But if one examines very carefully the general selective service, the food and war material rationing, if one scrutinizes the whole system which is now held in honour within the boundaries of our country, he cannot help seeing the great analogy with the policy which has been developed in Russia since Lenin, and especially after the accession of Stalin to power. I should like very much to know the names of the men responsible for this general economic policy, their connections in the world and their racial origin. Shall I be called isolationist if I ask the government to be very careful in the choice of its financial and economic experts, in order that this dominion will not be confronted with a system which will be in the hands of men not giving a thought to the country in which they operate, ignoring national boundaries, and ignoring the boundaries of nations, whether they be enemies or allies. This war will come to and end some day, and there will be another peace treaty written. The government then in power, with its experts, will suffer another Casablanca if these experts are not real Canadians having in mind the specific interests of Canada. Shall I be called isolationist if I point out that Canada will have to act as a nation of America before acting as a colony? The rate at which we are spending should cause us to have a system of collection toward the nations, especially those which might have in mind sooner or later the erasing of the war debts.
Shall I be called isolationist if I ask the government to stop and think for a moment that our agriculture is doomed if the farmers' sons are not sent back to the land? It is all very well for the government and its numerous propagandists to flash periodically the exemption of farmers' sons, but it is not so pleasant for the farmer to spend days and weeks begging the authorities to grant postponement, which is often granted after the boy has spent from four to six months in camp and is turned back to the land after the work is partly done or, in many instances, after the crop is lost. It is all very well for the provincial friends of the government to say,
The Address-Mr. Gauthier

we will have to be careful about the training of farmers' sons and farm help, but it would be better for those gentlemen to help those who have been urging the government to agree upon a specific policy toward agriculture in connection with military training. Why not exempt farmers' sons and farm help once and for all, and stop that flow of farmers to the commission? Let them work instead; and if they give to the cutting of wood fuel the time they are forced to spend in these trips to obtain delays from the military authorities, we should not have any shortage of this material. Let the government stop its policy of zig-zag. The farmers' sons have registered; why call them up at all?
I suppose I shall be called isolationist and opposed to the war effort if I tell this house that the work of women in war industries, especially where certain chemical products are used, is a crime against the families of this country? It is destroying a generation. What is more, if it is not stopped the next generation will be still-born. I am not the first one to give that warning to the government; a prominent doctor in Toronto gave a severe warning months ago.
That is the situation of this country, built up entirely by those who call us isolationists, to hide their real failure toward the true Canadian policy. If Canada is the granary for the united nations, it would have been wiser on the part of the administration to leave on the land those who by their patient and constant work can provide our allies with the necessary food. If, moreover, Canada is the arsenal of the allies, it would have been more prudent to organize the labour within the country than to cry out loud when hundreds of thousands of men are overseas. The trouble is that the small population of Canada was not taken into consideration. Only one thing mattered-to send men overseas. In the meantime the disorganization was increasing rapidly.
In 1939 we warned the government not to go too far and too fast. The answer was: moderate and voluntary effort. A year afterwards, one of our statesmen said in this house, "How can we participate in a war moderately?"
The war effort was changed into a total war effort. Conscription for Canada gave place to a disguised conscription for overseas service. Then, after the plebiscite, conscription was voted in this parliament under the pressure of the same men who just a few years ago were advocating a policy of no participation in any external war. And because we believe that this policy of no participation or of a moderate and voluntary effort should have been the real

Canadian policy, the same men disdainfully call us isolationists. What a transformation! They were first called isolationists by their Conservative friends, and after their secret marriage they found it an appropriate term by which to characterize those among their supporters who refuse to participate in the comedy built up by those who forsook the Canadian cause. I think that at the next election the people of this country are going to isolate some of these people from power.
It is no pleasure to be isolated. I had the experience of forty-four days of isolation at the citadel in Quebec. We were nine altogether under close arrest. Some of them are not yet out. Four men were still in the "clink" the day before yesterday, nearly four months after their arrest. Two of them are married, their families living on fresh water and public charity.
I do not question the respectability of the members of that public court-martial which opened in Quebec on November 22, 1942-I do not mean the final judgment; I do not discuss that-and none of the accused officers and men had any complaints against them. What has been unbearable for us and our families, for the medical profession and for our race is the pitiful lack of judgment leading to the decision to make the court-martial public. Since it was open to the public I shall make use of my privilege to say a few words about it.
The trial clearly proved that these men had not broken their oath either as soldiers or as medical men. They sold no blue papers-I mean discharges from the army-and did not give benevolent classification to any recruit to the active forces. These men have been under close arrest nearly all the time since the end of October for the non-commissioned officers and from November 2 for the medical officers. Three of the officers are free now and have resumed their duty in the army. One private was handcuffed for eleven days, day and night, and the three others for four days, day and night. When one realizes the hygienic conditions of the "clink" in the citadel, he can imagine the intolerable conditions which these men endured. Except for the exclusive privilege of being gently balanced at the end of a rope, or of enjoying the last moments of their lives while cosily seated in an electric chair, even killers do not undergo worse treatment.
The officers were under close arrest nearly all the time at the officers' quarters, each enjoying the steady presence of an escort. These were dangerous people facing that public trial! There was no bail for them.

The Address-Mr. Gauthier
For weeks and months they fed the newspaper chronicles and formed part of the radio journal, especially that of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation network. I was sorry for my prison mates to have been with them, because I immediately realized that it would be impossible for certain newspapers of my own and other provinces to resist the temptation to announce that a Quebec member of parliament was facing trial, that he was garbed in civilian clothes, and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation announcer even went so far as to say that I was wearing a brown suit, though he omitted to state the colour of my necktie. It was said that I was one of the lieutenants of Mr. Maxime Raymond, chief of the bloc populaire Canadien, the newly appointed organizer for the Quebec district, and so forth. Look at. the size of the type in the headlines. But I must be fair to the Ottawa Journal; when I was acquitted they gave me two good columns, with my picture-not the best I have, but, just the same, my picture.
What a start for a new movement; the organizer in gaol! What an advertisement for the Quebec medical profession; five of its members in gaol! What a good piece of French Canadian for some people to chew on! Why a public court martial in that case? To serve as an example; hobbling explanation. Apart from the thousands of other courts-martial that could have been held publicly in other districts in order to make examples, if that was the purpose, one was held in the same building at the same time, but it was held privately. Apparently it would not have been interesting to the public; the man was not from Quebec. I would not for a moment dare to think it was done for reasons of secrecy. The Quebec medical profession has no reason to envy the medical profession of any other province, or any other profession, and that public court-martial was an insult to the medical profession.
In a democracy the accused is innocent as long as the court has not found him guilty. The judges we have appointed have always respected this democratic principle. The way in which we were treated clearly proved that we were found guilty before the trial by those whose lack of judgment, be they in Ottawa or the advisers of the national defence department in the Quebec district, whose unfitness for the positions they hold in the medical corps or at headquarters made them the conscious or unconscious persecutors of respectable families and the slanderers of the medical profession and of French Canadians. I shall pass over the little war of nerves designed to bring the officers and men to a 72537-35
plea of guilty. That would have been such a nice feather in the caps of those who had smelled a big scandal and who, after the inquiry commenced, were obliged to put up a show to hide their incompetence from the courts and from their superiors. Let me quote Le Semaine Religieuse of Montreal, under date of January 20, 1943:
A Regrettable Court-Martial
(Translation): The court-martial of a group of medical men of Quebec has come to an end. Those hoping that something scandalous nature would come out of it were disappointed. The charges were light and in most cases definitely false. But the rumours which preceded this action and the publicity given to the charges have poisoned the minds from one end of the country to the other. Such doings can only hamper the national cause. It is regrettable that they occur.
I said a few moments ago that the people are tired, and I will add that in Quebec they are tired of being treated differently. There is a legal way of democratic election which they will use freely. The mention of the bloc populaire Canadien may bring a smile to someone's lips, but that smile will change into a grin when the youth of this country turns its back to its forsakers.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I represent a rural riding in this house. The people of Frontenac-Addington are among the finest people in this land, but they are not wealthy. They are good, honest, patriotic Canadian farmers who earn their living by hard work and the grace of God. Their standard of living depends upon the prices they receive for their products, and a few cents here or there may mean the difference between fair living and poor living. Thus they have felt grave concern over the treatment they have received since the beginning of this great struggle. They have not complained unduly; they have done their best to produce to their utmost in order to assist in the task of feeding our armed forces, our allies and our home population, but, as we all know, times before the war were not too good to them. Their farms had suffered and needed repairs, which could not be made. They had begged for parity prices, but to no avail; and then, when it seemed that their dream would be realized through the increased demand created by the war, ceilings were placed upon the prices of their products. This was not just. The ceilings should have been so adjusted that parity prices would prevail.
Parity prices to the farmer mean only one thing, namely, that he receives for his products the cost of production plus a reasonable profit. That is what industry is getting; that is what the farmer should get. Can he go on producing to the maximum without assistance in

The Address-Mr. Aylesworth

gome form? I do not think he can. He is growing older, and cannot work as hard. He has lost his sons and hired help to industry and the armed forces. His machinery is wearing out, and must be replaced if possible.
The farmer is in a position very much different from that of industry. Industry buys its raw materials, fabricates its products and fulfils its sales contracts in a matter of days or a few weeks. Production is not started until satisfactory sales arrangements have been completed. Delivery is then made before there is any general change in production costs.
That is not so, however, with the .farmer. His only guarantee of even the cost of production is his faith in the weather, God and the future-which in too many instances does not satisfy his banker. What is the prospect of meeting our food requirements in 1943? I should say it is hopeless unless something is done immediately to help the farmer. The year 1942 was, from a climatic point of view as nearly perfect as could be imagined. Although our supply of farm labour dwindled rapidly in 1942, yet during most of the year the longer hours on the farm, combined with increased work by men, women and children, resulted in the greatest production of food we have ever had. This was the condition, despite the fact that nearly 300,000 persons have been withdrawn from the farm labour supply since the beginning of 1940. Fuel supplies for trucks, tractors and other farm vehicles were not curtailed.
We do not know what Providence will give us by way of weather in the coming year, but we do know that in every other respect the capacity of the farmer to produce will be seriously curtailed if present policies are followed. Fuel will be scarce; the production of farm machinery is limited, and labour is much scarcer than last year. The men, women and children on the farms cannot work longer hours or do more than they did last year.
Then, farmers are also confronted with uncertainty as to whether, they will be able to secure prices which will enable them to meet the cost of production. Expenses of farm operation are constantly increasing. Wages are double. Prices of second-hand machinery are high. Taxes and other costs are increasing. We are confronted with the fact, too, that many farm units devoted to the production of most essential foods such as meats and dairy products have gone out of existence.
In addition to all these handicaps, many farmers are sincerely and honestly afraid to plan for their future farming operations for the simple reason that they do not know what further restrictions may be imposed. All hon.

members realize that while many untrained people can be very helpful in supplying labour on the farms, to meet the seasonal demands, still the maximum production requires the work of men of experience, men who are skilled in the art of producing and feeding live stock and poultry, men who are trained in respect of dairy production, crop production and the handling of modern machinery and equipment.
The practice of paying subsidies to avoid raising prices to the consumer cannot be fairly considered as preventing inflation, because the same total amount is paid, whether the consumer pays it all, or pays only part of it and the taxpayer the balance. I am utterly opposed to the use of subsidies in lieu of fair prices on the market place, particularly at a time when consumers are fully able to pay fair prices. Subsidies are inflationary. They conceal costs, and defeat their own purpose. They promote inefficiency, destroy initiative and undermine character. They are not the means of building an independent and self-reliant people. Subsidies are simply an expedient way of dodging a disagreeable issue. They are the means of evading a fundamental correction to an unbalanced economy. They open the way to political abuse. Once they are used, subsidies are hard to get rid of. If we employ them now, during a period of maximum income, how can we abandon them when the war is over and income falls? An empty treasury would mean that they would have to be dropped. Food prices would have to rise or the farmer would become bankrupt; this would involve rising food prices with declining purchasing power. I seek a free and self-supporting agriculture. The allocation of materials for the production of farm machinery must be also increased immediately. We need more machinery than usual to make up for labour shortages.
I should like now to discuss the beef situation. There is a price ceiling on beef, but I venture to say that most of the beef sold in Canada to-day is sold above the ceiling price. Speaking in this debate, the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Mills) referred to the black market on beef. No one knows better than he does that when he .sells his cattle for twelve cents a pound at the barn, the beef from those cattle is certainly not sold under the ceiling price. One need only look at the market report to find that good butcher cattle are selling at from 12 to 12J cents a pound live weight. These same cattle yield around fifty-six per cent in the killing. If they are sold under the price ceiling, the wholesaler would lose $25 a head or four cents a pound on the beef. For example, let us take a beef cow weighing 1,200 pounds. The wholesaler pays

The Address-Mr. Gray don
tea cents a pound, or $120 live weight. The 600 pounds of beef that he will get, at fifteen cents a pound ceiling, would net him only $90, or a loss of $30, or five cents a pound. I do not think he is taking that loss. If the government still holds to a ceiling on beef, then I suggest that it should be a fair and reasonable ceiling. The number of cattle shipped from western to eastern Canada for feeding and killing increased by 78-6 per cent in 1942; yet the number of inspected killings fell by 5-9 per cent. But there are no records of uninspected killings. Estimates place the increase in uninspected killings at 100 per cent.
On January 31, 1943, the Montreal Standard quoted the representatives of two leading packing houses in that city as saying that most Montrealers who were eating beef that week-end were eating the product of the black market. Why not raise the ceiling four or five cents a pound? The consumer would not have to pay any more than he is now paying. The spread at present between the producer and the consumer was never greater. The farmer must find it strange to have to pay high prices in the butcher shop for beef which has been sold under the ceiling.
Farmers who are feeding cattle this winter are worried. During the month of May, when the highest ceiling price will prevail, too many cattle will be placed on the market and, to my mind, this will force a drop in price. Some protection m>'st be given the cattle producer.
Butter is another product on which a ceiling might well be raised, so as to bring it on a par with cheese. Even to earn the 10-cent subsidy the butter fat must be taken to the creamery. In my constituency, with many of the roads blocked with snow, this cannot always be done, with the result that many of the farmers are letting their cows go dry this winter. Yet we are asked greatly to increase our production of milk. With money plentiful as it is to-day, most people will pay more in order to get butter, and thus another black market may spring up.
In line with the government's plan to increase food production this year, we should have the ban on new electrical connections lifted in order to permit extensions to additional farms and to allow short extensions of existing rural distribution lines to operate specified farm production equipment. It is to be expected that such extensions will among other things assist in increasing the country's supply of meats, poultry and dairy products, and in some measure relieve the farm labour shortage. It is the greatest help that could be provided to the Canadian farmer. Because too many rural people do not have what we 72537-35}
call the conveniences of life, it does not follow that they do not deserve them. Indeed, they do, and it is our job to see that the people on the land, upon whom the country relies in times of stress, are recognized according to their merits.
When this war is over, and I pray that it will be soon, we shall be called upon to help in feeding the millions of people who now have little food and will not have much for years to come on account of the scorched-earth policy and war-torn ground. It is possible to estimate that five hundred million people will be suffering from some degree of food shortage after this war and that some European countries such as Norway, Holland, France, Greece, Poland, Yugoslavia and the Baltic states will be much worse off than after the last war. Then twenty-seven million tons of food were supplied to Europe, sixteen million by the United States, and the rest by the British empire-food to the value of six billion dollars-and it will be many times greater this time. But we must furnish it. To save these millions after the war is not alone an act of compassion. It is the only road to peace.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, we urgently need to determine what we can do within our strength of man-power, materials, workshops and agriculture. We need to decide which of our tasks comes first, and if we determine rightly we shall place agriculture in the first rank of the war effort, alongside planes, guns and ships.
Our imperative necessity is maximum food production. The Canadian farmer will produce to the utmost if he is given a chance. The fate of the world may depend on it.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend at this stage of the debate to be very brief and to indicate to the house the position which the Progressive Conservative party will take with respect to the amendment to the amendment which was moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maelnnis).
Perhaps at the beginning of my remarks I may be permitted to read to the house the precise wording of the amendment to the amendment. It is as follows:
That the motion be further amended by adding to the amendment the following words:
"And further we regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to take the necessary action to achieve a total war effort by neglecting to apply the powers contained in the National Resources Mobilization Act to war industries
The Address-Mr. Graydon

and financial institutions in the same manner as they are being applied to the mobilization of man-power for military service."
In dealing with this amendment to the amendment I should like to call the attention of the house particularly to its very careful and considered phraseology. It indicates that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party takes the stand that with respect to two branches of our war effort, namely, war industry and war finance, the powers contained in the National Resources Mobilization Act should be applied. But the amendment goes further in its wording, which leaves no room for doubt. They want these powers applied "in the same manner"-and I call special attention to those four words-as these powers are being applied to the mobilization of manpower for military service.
The National Resources Mobilization Act gives wide and sweeping powers to the government to mobilize the human, material and financial resources of the nation for the purpose of waging total war. These are the broad powers, and assuming for the moment that the government has not applied these powers in the case of war industries and finance to the same extent as it might have done, consonant with the national interest in a war-time period, let us see how the proposed amendment to the amendment would assist in bringing us nearer to a total war effort than we now are.
Let us examine the results which would flow from the acceptance of the amendment to the amendment by the house. It would mean that from now on two great branches of our national war endeavour-war industry, and finance-would be mobilized "in the same manner"-mark those four words again-as is man-power for military service. In simple words, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation expresses implied satisfaction with the application of the powers of the National Resources Mobilization Act in so far as the mobilization of man-power for military service is concerned.
The people of Canada and the Progressive Conservative party believe, and I think there is plenty of evidence to substantiate such belief, that our whole man-power policy in Canada is a mess, a misfit and a muddle. In our opinion it is not possible to separate entirely in any effective, master man-power plan the mobilization of man-power for military service from that of any other part of the master man-power plan which should be in operation. Our objection is very strong on the point that no really over-all plan relating to our man-power has been in existence since the war began, whether it be for

military service, or agriculture, or other primary enterprises, or industry. We as a party will refuse to support an amendment to the amendment such as this, where the government's present muddling man-power policy is proposed to be used as a basis for the mobilization of war industry and finance. It would imply that our party is in favour of and is satisfied with the present man-power policy of the government-which it is not.
In every instance where a further mobilization of our war industries and finance is essential to the interests of a more extensive and total war effort, let us not hesitate vigorously to take those necessary steps as a nation, let the chips fall where they may; but when we do so, let us not take as our example the muddled policy which has been ineffectively and timorously applied to another branch of the wartime mobilization.
Were this very carefully drawn amendment to the amendment to carry, let us see what it would further mean. If the powers under the National Resources Mobilization .Act were to be applied to war industries and financial institutions in the same manner as they are being applied to man-power for military service, it might easily lead to hopeless confusion. I do not think this house would dare to support such a proposal, because the application of these powers to the mobilization of man-power for military service involves many points which cannot be logically and practically applied to the case of war industry and finance; yet the words "in the same manner" indicate that this is what the draftsman of this carefully worded amendment to the amendment and its mover and seconder had in mind.
Here are some of the implications which might readily result:
1.	Two important factors entering into the call-up of man-power for military service are age and condition of health. Surely the length of time a war industry or financial institution has been in business, or the state of its economic and financial health, cannot seriously be considered in applying "in the same manner" the man-power call-up provisions to these two other branches of our war effort. Yet that is what the wording "in the same manner" in the amendment to the amendment clearly indicates.
2.	It is said that one out of every 107 of our population in Canada has been mobilized under the provisions of the National Resources Mobilization Act. Surely, if war industries and financial institutions are to be mobilized for a total war effort in Canada, this would be

The Address-Division
a very puny percentage and could scarcely be regarded as an important contribution to our war effort generally.
3. The present man-power mobilization features of the National Resources Mobilization Act as at present applied call men for service within Canada only, or the territorial waters thereof. It is difficult to see how it could seriously be proposed that our war industries shall manufacture their materials of war for use within the territorial boundaries and limits of Canada and that shipments overseas should be on a purely voluntary basis; yet that is what the four words "in the same manner" seem to imply.
The amendment to the amendment, in our opinion, provides a faulty basis for the mobilization of our war industries and our financial institutions. It impliedly endorses the present muddled man-power policy of the government. It constitutes a retrograde and half-hearted step rather than an advanced move toward total war. It leaves us wffio represent a new Progressive Conservative movement with no option but to vote against it, in view of the definite and unequivocal policy laid down at the Winnipeg convention, which states:
We believe in the effective total utilization and proper allocation for war, by compulsion where necessary, of all the resources of Canada, including agriculture, industry and finance, as well as man-power, and that our aim should be at all times to bring about so far as human means can achieve it, an equality of sacrifice.
Upon that platform and that policy we stand. The present amendment to the amendment is a weak and feeble thing when contrasted with the war policy of the Winnipeg convention, and we cannot support it.

speechtext:
I do not intend to make any extensive remarks on the question which has been before the house for some days. The observations I made in the speech I last delivered laid down the principles and the premises upon which I propose now to base a conclusion. During all this debate it has been apparent to everyone in this house and to

everyone in the country who follows the debates of the House of Commons that we are suffering in Canada at the present time from an increasing shortage of man-power in so far as the farms are concerned, and at the same time the country is suffering from a shortage of man-power in our war industries, not to mention the fact that we are short of labour also in many other important and most essential industrial and transportation activities. Without going into any detail, I may mention rail transportation. I have been told recently by a man who is in a position to speak his own mind that they are afraid of running short of rolling stock on our railways in Canada. No one who has observed the situation has any doubt that there is a real shortage of man-power. Since the beginning of the debate, not a single member who has spoken has failed to draw the attention of the house and the country to the fact that we are short of labour in the main important fields of our activities. Therefore there can be no doubt that there is a very serious shortage of man-power. The suggestion has been made, and this indicates very well the truth of what I am now saying, that we should use prisoners of war, that we should use the Japanese, that we should use those who have been declared unfit for military service-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not in British Columbia.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
*-that we should use them where we are short of labour on the farms and in war industries as well as other essential industries of our country. So that the fact cannot be denied that there is a shortage.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon), as I said the other day, did not suggest a real remedy for the situation. He complained about the lack of a proper policy on the part of the government to meet the situation. He blamed the government for not having adopted a proper policy, but he did not say what in his opinion was a proper policy. He complained also about the situation in regard to labour but did not indicate in any definite terms what method and what means he had in mind as a remedy for the difficult situation in which the country finds itself at present. The amendment is so framed that it could be used in support of all shades of opinion.
I was accused in mild terms by the former house leader of the official opposition (Mr. Hanson) of arguing the case of the isolationists. I am not an isolationist; and if the hon. gentleman had taken the trouble to look at the record, he would have discovered that on many occasions I went a great deal further than he did in order to bring about and maintain unity between all

The Address-Mr. Cardin
parts of Canada. As a result I found myself in difficulties which he has never experienced. I think I have gone the limit in that regard; and with the people of my province and my race I have gone much further than he has ever gone in order to explain to them the sentiments, feelings and ideas of the citizens of, other sections of Canada. To the best of my ability I have tried to interpret the opinions and sentiments of the Englishspeaking people of Canada to the French citizens of the province of Quebec. I have done all I could, and I think all that any reasonable man could expect from a public man in my position.
I have been criticized in my own province for having preached the doctrine I did preach in 1939, supporting our participation in the war and asking the people of Canada to unite behind the government, to do all they possibly could in order to support the cause of the united nations. It was not a popular case to argue before the electors of the province of Quebec, but just the same I argued it; and when the general election came in 1940 I did the very same thing. I explained in clear language, without being afraid of expressing my views, what the position was at that time.
The late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, the late Hon. Fernand Rinfret and myself did all we could to help the people of the province of Quebec understand the necessities and exigencies of the situation in which Canada found- herself at that time. We succeeded then to a certain extent in interpreting the sentiments and the opinions of the Englishspeaking citizens of Canada.
I am proud to say that during my long political life I have never been afraid to voice my thoughts, and I have always devoted my energies and the limited talents that are mine in endeavouring to bring together as closely as possible the different races composing the population of Canada. I have suffered from this politically. I am still suffering from it, because some- people do not understand the position I have taken at certain times. They do not understand even now that I was attempting to fill the breach which existed between the two races, and trying to secure mutual -concessions in order to bring them together so that they would be happy, .prosperous and at peace within Canada. My attitude has been misrepresented even in this house by certain hon. gentlemen who have never been able to understand the situation with which the government was then confronted, and the position in which I personally was placed on many occasions.
I have always tried, to the best of my ability, and even by making personal sacrifices, to bring about a better understanding between all citizens of Canada. My voice has not always been heard, nor have my views been accepted in every case, but I am very happy to have heard lately, from the province of Ontario an echo of the views I expressed not very long ago, when I tried to explain that necessarily there was a difference in sentiment between the Englishspeaking citizens of Canada and the French Canadians. But few people understood my stand at that time, and my words were misrepresented or misinterpreted.
Just a few days ago, a gentleman enjoying a very high position in politics in the province of Ontario said in a public speech that we must recognize that we cannot see things in the same way because we are descendants of different races. And he said that he was not surprised that French Canadians do not always see the racial problems in the same light as English Canadians, because he could not feel the same way toward France as he does toward Britain. This is an echo of the sentiments I expressed, and I am very happy to record it; it is indeed for me a source of comfort.
I take second place to no one in this chamber or in the country as far as love for Canada is concerned, or as far as sacrifices are concerned. My patriotism is beyond question; my love for Canada is beyond question, and I have the right, as anyone else has, to state and explain my personal views in this House of Commons, where, thank God, we still enjoy a certain amount of liberty.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, and I may say as the conclusion of the premises I laid down in the speech I delivered the other day, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Dubuc), as an amendment to the amendment:
That all the words after the word "that" in the first line of the said amendment be struck out and that the following be substituted therefor:
"This house is of the opinion that in view of the recognized shortage of farm labour, also the admitted shortage of labour in war industries and in other essential industrial and transportation activities, Your Excellency's advisers should have provided for the withholding of the operation of the National Resources Mobilization Act in regard to the raising of men for military service until, at least, a complete investigation is made by a committee of the house, to ascertain and determine by what means or methods Canada can now most effectively contribute to the winning of the w'ar, without destroying the economic, social 4nd national life of the country."
